speaker: Chris Olah
title: What the hell is going on inside neural networks? | Chris Olah
question: In machine learning interpretability research, why do standard quantitative summary statistics and line plots often mislead researchers trying to understand how a neural network works?
guest: I think a lot of people conceive of science as studying summary statistics, because in a lot of science we have a couple of numbers we can boil things down to. People are often surprised by our work because they're used to machine learning research involving summary statistics and line plots, which feels very rigorous. But summary statistics can actually blind you. In Anscombe's quartet, you have sets of points with the same mean and standard deviation that look totally different when you actually look at them—and that's for two summary statistics we understand very well. There's so much intricate structure inside neural networks that if you try to boil it down to a single number before you understand what's going on, you lose sight of almost everything important. Sometimes people ask whether qualitative observations are scientific, like looking through a microscope and seeing cells for the first time—seeing cells was a qualitative result, not a quantitative one, yet it was very important. To really understand what's going on inside these models, you need to inspect fine-grained structure, which inevitably pushes you toward data visualization as a tool for accessing and navigating huge amounts of data.

points.core: Compressing complex neural network internals into aggregate numbers hides critical structural differences.
points.note: Accept: summary metrics like mean or accuracy masking completely different underlying distributions or mechanisms (e.g., Anscombe's quartet). Do not credit: generic claims that metrics can be gamed or surface mentions of visualization being prettier.

points.core: Choosing meaningful quantitative metrics requires first understanding the system's underlying qualitative structure.
points.note: Accept: needing exploratory qualitative observation before boiling behavior down to numbers, or comparing early interpretability to microscopy discovering cells. Do not credit: generic praise of qualitative research or both-sides hedging that both qualitative and quantitative matter.

points.core: Rich visual interfaces are necessary to sift through massive high-dimensional model data.
points.note: Accept: using bespoke data visualization or interactive inspection tools to navigate large parameter or activation spaces directly. Do not credit: vague claims that charts aid communication to lay audiences or standard training-loss plotting.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Summary statistics and line plots mislead because they compress a high-dimensional, highly structured object into a few numbers, and that compression discards exactly the structure interpretability is trying to find.

A single scalar such as mean loss, accuracy, or average activation averages over many data points, neurons, and mechanisms. Very different underlying behaviors can produce the same number, as Anscombe's quartet illustrates for ordinary statistics. A network might solve a task with several distinct algorithms on different input subsets, or a neuron might fire for unrelated reasons, and an aggregate hides this heterogeneity. Rare but important cases, outliers, and multimodal distributions vanish in the mean.

These metrics also only answer the question you thought to ask. Choosing a statistic bakes in a hypothesis about what matters, so they can confirm or deny an expectation but rarely reveal something unexpected. A smooth curve can therefore create false confidence in a wrong mechanistic story.

This is why researchers such as Chris Olah argue for looking at the raw detail: individual examples, per-neuron activations, attention patterns, and rich interactive visualizations, with summary statistics used afterwards to test hypotheses formed that way.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Standard summary statistics and line plots compress high-dimensional, richly structured neural computations into low-dimensional scalars, discarding the very mechanistic details interpretability seeks to uncover. Because interpretability remains largely pre-paradigmatic, researchers often do not yet know the right abstractions or natural units to measure. Consequently, scalar metrics—such as average sparsity, reconstruction error, or mean ablation effects—act only as rough proxies that project an illusion of statistical rigor while masking qualitative reality. Averaging across inputs or components routinely cancels out opposing, context-dependent effects and obscures heavy-tailed distributions, polysemantic neurons, and distinct circuit structures, allowing fundamentally different internal algorithms to produce identical curves. Relying on line plots also invites Goodhart-style pitfalls: in sparse dictionary learning, for instance, a regularization change like tanh penalties can improve quantitative sparsity–reconstruction curves while quietly introducing degenerate or split features, which researchers only catch through direct qualitative inspection of individual features and circuits.

noweb.answer:
Standard summary statistics and line plots often mislead interpretability researchers because neural networks compute through high-dimensional, heterogeneous, and nonlinear mechanisms that aggregation inherently obscures. Averaging metrics—such as mean neuron activations, aggregate feature attributions, or overall accuracy—collapses distinct subpopulations and competing internal circuits into a single deceptive trend, much like Anscombe’s quartet. A neuron or attention head may appear unimportant on average while firing decisively on rare inputs, or encode multiple unrelated concepts through polysemanticity and superposition whose effects wash out in expectation.

Similarly, smooth loss or probing curves frequently mask abrupt algorithmic phase transitions, pockets of outlier memorization, or reliance on brittle spurious shortcuts that fail out of distribution. Low-dimensional line plots also force distributed, entangled representations onto preselected axes, hiding the cooperative geometric interactions across layers and components that actually carry meaning. Most importantly, passive summary metrics capture statistical correlation rather than causal structure, confounding incidental activation byproducts with the computations driving a prediction. Understanding how a network truly works therefore requires granular, input-level inspection and targeted causal interventions rather than aggregate averages.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Summary statistics and line plots mislead because they compress a high-dimensional, heterogeneous system into a few numbers. Neural network behavior usually isn't uniform, so the compression hides the structure researchers are trying to find.

An average over a dataset can blend several distinct mechanisms, outlier cases and subpopulations into one value that describes none of them. This is the Anscombe's-quartet problem: very different underlying patterns can produce the same mean, variance or correlation. Neurons are often polysemantic, so a neuron's average activation or a feature's mean attribution can look meaningful while actually reflecting several unrelated features at once. Aggregate loss curves can look smooth while specific tokens or skills go through sharp phase changes, as when induction heads form. Line plots add a second problem: connecting points suggests a continuous, ordered relationship along the x-axis, such as layers, neuron indices or checkpoints, even when no such structure exists.

The practical lesson is to look at the raw data directly. That means examining individual examples, full distributions, scatter plots and dataset examples before trusting summaries that can confirm a hypothesis while hiding what the network is actually doing.

models.answer: Standard quantitative summary statistics and aggregate line plots often mislead interpretability researchers because they compress high-dimensional, nonlinear computations into a few low-dimensional numbers, stripping away the actual mechanisms driving a model's behavior. Averaging across thousands of neurons, layers, or data points masks crucial heterogeneity: a network may rely on entirely different internal circuits, heuristics, or spurious shortcuts across different subpopulations, yet still produce smooth, reassuring aggregate curves. Furthermore, single-number metrics and trend lines frequently suffer from observational equivalence, where vastly different internal algorithms yield identical loss, accuracy, or probe scores. Smooth aggregate trends can also conceal abrupt underlying phenomena, such as phase transitions, feature superposition, or polysemantic neurons shifting roles, creating a false impression of simple, continuous dynamics. Ultimately, because these summaries measure correlational outcomes rather than causal structure, they invite confirmation bias and make it easy to mistake surface-level statistical fit for genuine mechanistic understanding of how the neural network computes its answers.

points.why: The response explicitly explains how identical aggregate scores can hide distinct internal mechanisms.
quotes: vastly different internal algorithms yield identical loss, accuracy, or probe scores

points.why: The response critiques aggregate metrics but never says that qualitative exploration should guide metric selection.
The response identifies the high dimensionality of model internals but never proposes rich visualization or interactive inspection to navigate them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Summary statistics average over inputs, tokens, or neurons, so they can hide the cases that reveal how a network works. A feature that activates strongly in a narrow context can look unimportant on average, and two networks with nearly identical scores can rely on different cues. Line plots can preserve some of that averaging while adding a visual suggestion of smooth change, even when the underlying behavior varies sharply across contexts.

The deeper issue is that an observational pattern can have several mechanistic explanations. A neuron’s activation might track a prediction because it helps produce it, or because both depend on the same upstream computation. Looking at individual examples and breaking results down by context helps uncover what the summaries hide. Targeted interventions can then test whether changing a component changes the prediction as the proposed explanation would imply.

points.why: The response shows how averaging can hide context-specific features and how similar scores can conceal different mechanisms.
quotes: A feature that activates strongly in a narrow context can look unimportant on average
two networks with nearly identical scores can rely on different cues.

points.why: The response uses individual examples to investigate existing summaries and leaves unexplained how qualitative understanding should guide the choice of metrics.
The response proposes inspecting examples and testing components but does not explain how rich visual interfaces help researchers navigate high-dimensional model data.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Summary statistics and line plots can accurately describe a pattern while hiding how the network produces it. An average can make a feature look unimportant when it strongly affects a small group of inputs, or when its effects on different inputs cancel out. A line connecting layer averages can suggest that the network builds up a signal gradually, even if the signal appears abruptly at different layers for different inputs.

The deeper issue is that different mechanisms can produce the same statistic or curve. For example, a feature’s activation may track a prediction because both depend on the same input cue. The correlation alone cannot tell whether the network uses that feature to make the prediction. Examining individual cases can reveal what the summary conceals, and targeted interventions can test whether a proposed mechanism actually affects the output.

points.why: The response explains how averaging across inputs can make abrupt changes at different layers appear gradual.
quotes: different mechanisms can produce the same statistic or curve
the signal appears abruptly at different layers for different inputs

points.why: The response recommends examining individual cases but does not explain why qualitative understanding should guide the choice of quantitative metrics.
The response proposes case inspection and interventions without connecting rich visualization to navigating large, high-dimensional model data.
